extracted.intended_audience: students of political philosophy, legislators, statesmen, and readers of classical political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for classifying, designing, and judging constitutions and regimes: which persons or laws should hold supreme power, how states arise from social composition, and what practical requirements a legislator must meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law as reason without desire
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws should be dispassionate and not guided by appetite or favour; passion influences those in power even if they are good, so entrusting decisions to law prevents arbitrary acts motivated by hatred or friendship. The moral law is superior to written law, and written law is safer than entrusting everything to individual judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best law versus best man
rubrics_metrics.description: Enquire which is preferable, that the best man or the best law should govern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws can cover many matters impartially, but cannot cover everything; for cases outside written law some person(s) must decide. Prefer laws when they suffice, but recognise legitimate space for magistrates to rule where laws are silent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer many magistrates to one where discretion is required
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to have many than one to decide cases which cannot come under written law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple decision‑makers reduce individual partiality and error ('one person cannot see better with two eyes than many can with many'). Absolute rulers counter this by creating many assistants (eyes, ears, hands) — a reason to prefer distributed authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place supreme power in excellence (virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: When some family or individual so far excels in virtue as to exceed all others, it is right that kingly power should be in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptional virtue justifies ongoing supreme power rather than rotation; it would be unnatural and unjust to ostracise or reduce the highest to the lowest. This supports monarchic rule where excellence is concentrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and morals produce good rulers and citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Education and morals are almost the whole which go to make a good man; the same qualities will make a good citizen or good king.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A polity's quality depends on the moral and educational formation of its rulers and citizens; cultivating virtue is central to establishing the best government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator must know the ideal, the practicable, and the corrupt forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator ought to be acquainted not only with that which is most perfect imaginable, but also that which is best suited to given circumstances, and to discern and correct corrupt or imperfect forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical lawgiving requires understanding ideal constitutions, the varieties of existing governments, how forms arise and corrupt, and simple attainable institutions; correcting an established government's mistakes is as important as conceiving an ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame laws to fit the state, not fit the state to the laws
rubrics_metrics.description: All laws are, and ought to be, framed agreeable to the state that is to be governed by them, and not the state to the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different kinds of oligarchies and democracies require different laws; a one‑size‑fits‑all statute-book is inappropriate. Lawgivers must tailor institutions to social composition and customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify governments by who holds supreme power
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments are distinguished as kingly, aristocratical, or free states, according to where the supreme power is placed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classificatory criterion underpins further distinctions and helps identify the corresponding corrupt/degenerate forms (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy as excesses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise corresponding perverted/excessive forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Each good form has an excess: kingly→tyranny, aristocratic→oligarchy, free state→democracy (as a perversion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate regimes by how they deviate from their virtuous principle; tyranny is the worst excess, oligarchy the next, and democratic excess the least harmful among these perversions (disputed by earlier writers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of democracy and oligarchy by who participates
rubrics_metrics.description: A democracy is when the supreme power is in the hands of the freemen; an oligarchy when it is in the hands of the rich.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic numerical definitions: the many vs few is related but secondary. Consider eligibility rules, census thresholds, and whether the law or majority-vote exercises supremacy when classifying a regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of law as criterion of a free state
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the government is not in the laws, there is no free state; the law ought to be supreme over all things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If decisions rest on majority votes and not on settled laws, demagogues take power and the people can act tyrannically; a polity where law, not transient popular will, governs is properly 'free'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different species arise from distribution of social parts
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many sorts of governments because each city consists of many parts (families, rich, poor, husbandmen, artificers, merchants, soldiers, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxonomy of regime types should account for which social groups share in government: who supplies soldiers, who engages in commerce, who holds wealth—variations produce distinct species of democracy, oligarchy, aristocracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of democratic species
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple democratic species exist: equality‑based (law-directed equality), census‑based (magistracy by small census), government in the laws, universal‑citizen participation, and people‑governed majority rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each form differs in eligibility, whether the law or majority rules, and in practical causes (e.g., public revenue, paid attendance leading to poor domination). Distinguish democracies by how offices are filled and whether laws restrain popular impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of oligarchic species
rubrics_metrics.description: Several oligarchies: office by census (excluding poor); magistrates of small fortune filling vacancies; hereditary nobility; and oligarchy unchecked by law (a dynasty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oligarchies may evolve: concentration of wealth and office can lead from legal oligarchy to hereditary dominance and eventually to monarchical/dynastic rule when law is supplanted by persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of magistrates for cases beyond written law
rubrics_metrics.description: No one denies that it is necessary that there should be some person to decide those cases which cannot come under the cognisance of a written law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While laws should be primary, legislators must provide for competent magistrates (preferably multiple) to interpret and decide exceptional matters; institutional mechanisms for discretionary adjudication are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: A city must be self-sufficient with necessary functional parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A city is made up of different parts — husbandmen, artisans, merchants, hired labourers, soldiers, rich patrons, office‑holders — and must be self‑sufficient; without a military it is not a proper city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of constitutional roles must recognise necessary economic and military functions; institutional allocation of offices should reflect these roles and ensure capacity for defence and provisioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy as rule by the best on virtuous principles
rubrics_metrics.description: An aristocracy is a state governed by the best men, upon the most virtuous principles, where a man is both a good man and a good citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocracy is the ideal form when virtue is the organising principle; there are secondary forms where virtue coexists with wealth or citizenship, producing different hybrid regimes (e.g., Carthaginian, Lacedaemonian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of demagogues and comparability to tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: When the people rule by vote unchecked by law, demagogues arise and the people's decrees resemble tyrants' edicts; the people under demagogues are like tyrants supported by flatterers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware systems where collective will substitutes for law: such systems concentrate despotic power in assemblies and promote sycophancy and attacks on magistrates that undermine stable rule of law.
